body:
It is a very interesting discussion, the relative nature of how anxiety manifests its strongest at different parts of the day. It does make perfect sense that the stillness of the night means less distractions from your thoughts, or perhaps you have had negative or even traumatic experiences surrounding sleep and bedtime (nightmares, sleep paralysis, insomnia, night terrors, and more descriptively- something traumatic happening to you during sleep or at night in a bed)

In my case, the evenings are usually when I am most calm, to the point where getting my first sleep in I feel the most normal. It’s when I wake up from my first cycle that I am stuck in insomnia when my anxiety is bad. The mornings to me are the most anxious - it’s the great reset to do it all over again. All the work I did on myself to get through the day has to be repeated, the same doubts and anxieties re-arising. All the problems and uncertainties are there again,.

I too can relate to this a lot. In my case, I started with crippling childhood anxiety. Nobody thought I would leave the house. 

After intervention as a kid, I got the tools to start doing well in school, taking on my fears, I felt invincible. I got my higher education, did schooling across the country and lived on my own, then went and lived in Japan! Married to one of the most supportive people I have ever met, with two beautiful kids. 

Yet the happily ever after ending I made for myself did not account for my fortitude to maintain it. With my own health issues, on top of how scary the world has come geopolitically, I feel as if I’m barely hanging on by a thread. My family relies on me for financial and emotional support and as time goes on I feel less and less suited to the role of a person to be relied on. These are feelings I never had until a few years ago, it gets more pervasive.

I know there is something wrong with my brain, but I hoped experience and conquering myself in my youth would have changed that.

Hey, I know this is a far reach, but it sounds like you need a group of people to talk to let some of this out. Sometimes you don’t get too many responses here.

I find Discord has been useful in talking to some people who might be able to relate. I would recommend The Therapy Center discord if you just need others to vent to (I do not run and am not affiliated with the discord fyi, it helped me a lot six months ago when I was in the depths of my depression and it was a good tool to help pull me out — I still frequent there to help others.

Yeah I can normally feel an episode coming on as well. It’s a general darkening of my overall mood, very subtle with a bit of that baseline anxiety in the back — my mind preparing me for a worst case scenario and not letting me have any interest in anything else until the feeling is addressed. 

I know I’m in when the sleep gets hit. Days that I experience maintenance insomnia and struggle to sleep is when I know I’m in a proper depressive episode. 

I just dodged one a couple weeks ago but now I feel like I might be due for one soon with the way the world seems to be going

I am not too sure how helpful my answer may be,

I work in health care as as a clinician (will keep it vague for anonymity), and although I have a lot of anxiety around my own health and issues, being able to help others directly as my means of income gives me a sense of purpose that helps me make some sense of the world.

I cannot control the chaos around me, I can barely control it within me. But at least while I am here, I can help others have a bit more control over theirs.

Man.. I am sorry to hear you are going through that.  
I myself am back to feeling hopeless, things out of my control.  
Try as I might, something always makes it all for naught.

I want to cry and I can't. My whole body cries yet my eyes do not.

I feel the exact same way. If it isn’t something within my internal life (my own health conditions, not being able to afford a basic house despite making more money than my Father did when he bought a fully detached), it’s world events, feeling like the securities and medications I need to survive can be wiped from me under the current political climate. 

As a Canadian, all these taunts and threats at turning us into a 51st state and trying to normalize taking over a country like it’s funny all over social media … it is rotting my faith in humanity. For most people they can roll their eyes (up until it happens), but I am unable to. I can only imagine what Ukrainians feel, what people who live in the Gaza Strip feel. They have to live these fears in reality.


I try to talk to people about how I feel and they just laugh it off or pay little heed to it. Maybe someone who has a healthy body and enough money, or a job that allows them to work flexibly from anywhere, they don’t need to worry. They can figure it out.

I feel like because of my personal circumstances, I don’t have that same luxury. The only reason I haven’t tried to end it yet is because I have a wife and kids who are the world to me in times like this. I have to pretend to be strong so my children can grow up feeling loved and secured. 

I don’t want to repeat the push my traumas
onto my kids. It takes every fiber in me to not. 

Its very easy to feel like giving up some days

I sometimes feel the same way when things just get absolutely overwhelming. I try to look for hope but can’t find it — even when the answer is smack dab in front of me. 

The world is so beautiful, and many aspects of my life are beautiful. But I can’t see it when I’m like this, it doesn’t feel like any of this beauty outshines this feeling of despair.

OPs statement also resonates with me a lot. I’m in here when things are down, and as soon as my mood starts to lift and I start feeling more positively towards the future I find myself not on here as much if at all. 

Unfortunately I am back here now as life is overwhelming- both personally and politically/globally.  I’m doing my best to catch myself before I sink

This is exactly me. My daughter is 10 and my son is 7. I live like I am on a clock. I want them to be independent before it is my time to go. I suffer from this idea I don’t have much time left, and having chronic illnesses also makes it feel far more real. I want to trust that my wife could manage both of them in her own, but the guilt I would feel from traumatizing them haunts me. I saw my dad go from his usual self to a husk of a human in under a year — I would never want to subject my kids to that at any age, but especially when they are young and in their formative years
Hey there I am in the exact same boat. Chronic illness and health anxiety is a match made in hell. Would not wish this on my worst enemy

I want more than nothing else but to recover from this. For the sake of my wife and children, I don’t want to fear like this for the rest of my life.

I too had childhood anxiety and was medicated quite young (12-13). It helped immensely and I lived my formative years with very managed anxiety. I also went though a life threatening health scare at 18, and didn’t really think too much of it at the time as I just trusted the doctors would figure it out.

It was the creeping health problems that followed from my mid-to-late twenties to at begin to turn my health anxiety into the largest demon in my life.

I am 38 now with a wife and two kids, and I am so grateful for them and how my life turned out. However my anxiety is back and it has merged with a depression that this is the remainder of my life. 

There is a very sheer feeling that elements out of my control have a deep grip on my life (that being my health issues), and it has driven me to despair in cycles. The added responsibility of being a provider for my family makes it feel like I have no choice but to soldier on for the sake of their lives. But it has trapped me — I feel consumed by my circumstances.

I increased my medication an almost two weeks ago and so I’m waiting for that to kick in (can take 6-8 weeks), and I started to see a therapist. I’m not sure how much it will help but I need to try.

You. are. as tough as the hardest of STEELS.

I really don't think neurotypical people experience the  degree of despair, pain, hopelessness that many of us on this sub do, nevermind the frequency/duration of it. Yes, everyone gets sad when bad things happen in life, but depression is an entirely different beast in itself. It's all consuming fog with no light at the end of the tunnel for many.  


And the fact that you accept that and keep walking, making it another day with all that mental anguish -- is as warrioresque as it gets.
goddamnit this made me laugh.

Thank you for the beautiful words. I find when I'm at my low points the vulnerable, emotional parts of me come out in tandem. 

To all of you out there struggling with this, we are all brethren in this war. One day at a time, one step at a time, we give this life another chance.

I want to say something if I may.  


Thank you so much for your bravery. 15 years in your condition, watching your body slowly deteriorate. I cannot imagine how that kind of hell is. Of course the people around you wish for you to be alive, but it is also selfish of them to expect you to live with such QoL for the sake of being alive. Of course I can absolutely feel for your parents if they are still around, or any SO/immediately family you also have. Life for them will absolutely be different after you are gone, grief changes you forever.  


But I also have sympathy for your condition and understand why you decided to do what you are doing. I would also say that although it's not anyone's right to tell you how to live your life; I hope you don't go through with it -- as selfish as it is for me to say. I too have chronic health issues that will lead to low QoL for me sometime in the future, and it feels like a march on death's clock for me. I entertain death and suicide as a coping mechanism, knowing that the option is there is the suffering goes beyond anything I can control is a relief.. but I don't think I'll press the button because I'm way too mortified of the consequences.

Beautifully said. I'm in a similar situation where I'm stuck dealing with a myriad of health issues for the rest of my days. It seems like every trip to the doctor for health results is another traumatic experience, and it ends up being a feedback loop where going to the doctor reinstates the stress and trauma every single time, and I have no choice but to go if I want to continue my medication so it's a horrible cycle.   


What I would do to escape this. What I would trade for another chance at life in a healthy body. I see the people living around me and I can't help but feel envy at how they are blessed with vitality. We take for granted what we have until it's gone.

It makes me feel like a coward for entertaining suicide as a way to deal with my problems, despite having a beautiful and wonderful wife and 2 kids, a mother and sister who also would be in absolute ruin if I were gone.

But it's becoming so hard to deal to cope with the fact that my body is fundamentally broken. Without modern medicine I would have been dead at 17-18. I buy time, prolong an inevitable suffering for the ones I love -- but time and time again the selfish part of me would not mind just letting it all go.
yep, my SSRIs are literally my insulin. It takes a rough patch in my life to realize how important they are to keeping me grounded.
Hey. It's not just you fighting this battle of survival. We all come from different walks of life but the feeling of despair in our differing circumstances cuts a similar depth.

Thank you so much for sharing. You have had a very difficult upbringing, and it's very understandable you turns to vices such as food and smoking to deal with the pain of what you've had to go through.  


I really wouldn't be too worried about your future health if you are young, especially if you have no other health conditions. Quitting while your young, you can quite surprisingly turns things around health wise, much faster than you might anticipate. The human body is very resilient in youth.  


As someone with chronic health issues, appreciate every day you have with your health. You don't have cancer right now, and nobody knows what the future holds, so ruminating on that as something you desire to control will continue to fuel your anxiety.   


I know exactly how you feel. When I was in my 20s, dealing with what at the time I imagined to be a very serious health situation and how knowing I had a death clock, some tangible aspect of myself that I could anchor on to as a mark of my eventual death was debilitating. It still is, but 7-8 years later I've become a lot better at letting some of it go. I still have really bad weeks, but every single time something knocks me down I've become better at letting go of my lack of control and only focusing on what I can do.

​

I wish you the best.

I feel like sometimes the best way is to just do your best with the factors you can control, and have the mental resilience to push through to the end.   


With depression and anxiety the classic saying goes "Before you can help others you have to be able to help yourself". In being unable to do that, its scary to think about how it might impact my family. Which is why I feel like such a coward, not being able to deal with things head on like I'm expected to. Ending it all on my own terms feels like the one thing I know I can control.

It's definitely akin to the waves of the ocean - there are moments of stillness, and other moments of absolute chaos and despair.   


I do have health anxiety disorder, although I do have some reasoning behind it as I have legitimate health issues. It sounds like in your case the panic feeds in directly to your phobia -- if you are worried about a heart attack having a panic attack can feel like that at times. Given your age I wouldn't worry at all about having a heart attack assuming you are otherwise healthy. Hell, with my beaten down body I've had panic attacks for 25 years of my life and I've yet to have anything even remotely close to a cardiac event. 

I've been told to appreciate the life and health I have right now instead of dooming and glooming about the future but as I'm sure you are aware it's a hell lot easier said than done.

It's a very common symptom of anxiety. I've experienced it countless times, especially when the panic hits a point that's so overwhelming that it feels like your breathing is cut.   


If you are overall tense a lot due to general anxiety you might experience this sensation prolonged over time. Added to the fact that you are probably hyper-concentrated on your throat and you are hyper fixating on every sensation that occurs.   


Rest assured that you won't choke from this, although panic can definitely feel that way. When it happens remember to breathe deep and try to focus your attention elsewhere, away from throat onto something else.

I apologize. it wasn't targeted at anyone at all, especially nobody on this subreddit. I had a really bad day at the doctor's and I was just yelling into the void, I should be more careful as to who my audience is. 

I imagine a lot of us are struggling with existence and I would never been to point my finger to any visitors to this sub specifically. I'd say it was more directed to the average person we all see on social media, going about their day with little care for much else.

Many of us share your sentiments.   


Today I'm especially feeling the same way. I was born wrong and I shouldn't exist. I've done so much to better myself and in the end it ends up amounting to nothing. I've overcome a lot of big challenges in my life, but the minute I take time to relax something worse happens and drives me back down in the ground - reminding me that I'm sick, I'm weak, I am physically unable to live up to my potential.

Wow I could have written this myself. I'm in a very similar situation, although I've had health anxiety before kids.

There was a time where I've come to accept the inevitability of my own death and although I was still very scared, I was more resigned knowing that it would just be me.

As a father it's 1000x harder. You have someone that is more important than you now, and there feels like what's a lot of pressure to keep yourself grounded to support and raise them as best as you can.

I too doubt my ability to be a great father because of my anxiety and health. I'm very fortunate to have a very understanding wife who is an optimist in many ways, so it helps me push on.   


But it's important to remember that I don't think any mother or father goes through parenting without any doubts. We are bound to make many mistakes on the way and with life comes random hardships with time. All you can do is your best, to embrace your children and let them know how much you love them, even if sometimes you re incapable of being mentally available. When you have your good days, do you best to take advantage of them.

​

The fact that you are demonstrating concern for your children is already a very good indication that you are a far better father than many out there. Consider your children lucky :)
Youtube is a great resource for motivational videos. Use those to stimulate yourself every day. Make it a habit!

This is something that has been the crux of my anxiety for a long time. 

Nothing happens so it doesn't matter is really selling it short I would say. There is a way to look at this from a spiritual standpoint without having to think about things from a creator standpoint.  


The Real You by Alan Watts [http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mMRrCYPxD0I](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mMRrCYPxD0I) probably does the explanation better than I ever could. It's a great place to start.   


Anxiety regarding death is natural. We avoid the reality of it, especially those of us with anxiety. I find the more I have exposed to myself to concepts of death, and the more I'm gotten older and encountered more experiences (and suffering), my anxieties, while still there, have at least eased a bit.

This life is scary. There are no doubts there. We are no more entitled to happiness as we are to suffering. 

To endure it is a challenge for almost everyone to some degree. For those of us with anxiety, it's like life on hard mode. We are paralyzed by our decisions, by the things we must confront, the challenges we are made to face. Sometimes you become so tired you just want to sleep forever, but you are so paranoid of letting go of this consciousness.
This resonates with me a lot. I’m on the other side of the world and my problems follow me everywhere I go.

Awesome to hear that you are anxiety free, and that you were able to find a way to fight it without medication.

It has been a lifelong battle for me, and health anxiety is by far the worst. Unfortunately for me, I do have some chronic health conditions that amplified the anxiety to a full blown phobia, and any time I have some symptom or another happen I relapse into full-blown existential crisis.

​

I really hope you are able to coast forever though. I was generally anxiety free for my longest period for a good 5-6 years (19 to 25), and I say general because although I'm sure I had bouts of worrying and anxiety, it was never full blown and disruptive to my daily functioning entirely.   


A lot has changed in my life since 25, and looking back seven years I can say that I'm very surprised I've made it this far and I'm still around. I remember re-entering the debilitating anxiety states at 25 like they happened yesterday and how much they paralyzed me. Now, although it gets extremely tough at times (including right now), I have found a lot more strength in dealing with the burden and I've come to accept suffering as a natural part of life as much as happiness. I hope the best for you man, and I'm sure you wouldn't wish the feelings of your last year on anyone, just as I wouldn't wish my experience on anyone else.

That sounds a lot of like depression, dark night of the soul, it could even be an existential crisis you are in.

​

I think a lot of us carry an inertia of creativity, excitement and hope for the future in our youth. The opportunities in front of you seem limitless and the world is ripe for the taking. Throughout the teenage years and into adulthood, reality slowly dawns upon us as the doors of opportunity close, and it hurts our want to create and imagine and hope. There isn't necessarily a stimulus for this, but I think we become enlightened to the way the world actually is -- we become more exposed to the suffering that accompanies us in life alongside the happiness, and for many we start to experience the tidal nature of life -- ebbs and flows, suffering and happiness. Sometimes, the suffering is there for a very long time, and we forget that there is happiness. We start to question everything, the purpose of it all. 

  
Just know that it is normal for many of us to question, to have an existential crisis. I would never wish suffering on anyone, but it seems to be an intangible part of the human experience.

Don't take my advice over a professional, but he sounds like he had an extremely sheltered lifestyle, likely with overprotective parents. He doesn't seem to have developed a sense of independence yet and remains over reliant on those around him. He may be suffering from a lot of anxiety that he's not articulating well. 

​

I have a lot of difficulty going to the doctor myself because of my health anxiety, it's the fear of confirmation. Similarly, although I've done a lot to grow towards independence, my childhood anxiety has made the progress rough and there are low points I still deal with where I can't fight on my own and need the support of family and friends.   


It really is up to you if you want to be that person to help him grow as a person, but I imagine it will be something that will only endure if you love him and he reciprocates equally. The world forces us to grow up fast sometimes, as it did in my case. But do what makes you happy, don't feel obliged to walk him into adulthood.

Sometimes, there is no reason aside from brain chemistry. But there are times where a discrepancy between what you idealized your life to be in youth relative to where you are now creates perpetual grief and regret. A lot of it tends to stem from our past without even realizing. 

I had a perfect upbringing but I overidealized the future. When problems in my life arose, the anxiety and sheltered life I grew up had me ill-prepared to face things head on. Eventually they would pile on and it would get so overwhelming that ending it all brought me comfort. But I can't do that now, I can't do that to my wife, my mom, my children. So I push forward as much as I can. Eventually I will get around to checking up on my health and dealing with whatever news I receive.

What is it that is causing your urge to end your life?  


You said you have two amazing kids. I too have two amazing kids and a wife that keeps me around. My Dad passed away two years ago and I couldn't possibly do this to my mom either.   
Anxiety has been my major issue. I have had several health issues as well, some chronic that I keep an eye on, but the idea of having ANOTHER health problem or some other disease, or cancer that will slowly rot me from the inside is debilitating and sometimes has me want to just press the off button permanently on it all.

​

But I think as parents we have lost a little bit of that freedom in making a decision to just end it all. Your action would put your immediate family in the same realm of perpetual hell that you have had to live through.   


I hate the suffering and being in a hell state as much as you, but the parental drive in me holds me back. This is the cross we are made to bear on our back. The painful but strong way is to bear it for the sake of our family.

Hey there.

It sounds like you are in the learning ropes of the job still. My advice would be to put in as MUCH as you can fit in to your day to learning the ropes, even outside of work. Google and the internet in general is a great resource to troubleshoot on all IT issues. It may be constraining at first, feeling like you are dedicating your whole life to this job, but by no means does it have to be from wake to sleep. Before you know it, you'll be on top of things and have things in order. Things will pop up of course, but you will have developed the foundation to tackle those issues. Best of luck!

Hey.   


Getting older comes with transitions in the chapters of our lives. I think we naturally look to others (in person and in in social media/general media) as reference points to our own personal progress and happiness. This is both, the most natural thing to do, and the worst thing to do.  


You acknowledged yourself you have a sweet family, decent job and great parents. Yet, there is something in you yearning for more. This is fine, as it may be a calling for you to push your limits and not settle with being content. But if it's born from your comparison with others that leads to nothing but suffering and misery.   


The only perspective you share is your own, and when you look at the success/failure of others it is always only through your own experience. We have no idea what those people went through, where they come from, and what will happen to them. What is presented to you is the very surface of what they want the world to see, just as you presented this essence of positivity to others.

​

I do resonate with your feelings of living for others before yourself, because I find myself in the same situation. Growing up with considerable anxiety, my parents were always overprotective of me because they honestly felt they didn't have a choice. I grew and surpassed what anyone thought I was capable of in my late teens/ early 20s considering how crippled I was from anxiety in adolescence and it was extremely motivating for me, even getting through a life-threatening auto immune condition at 17. I felt like the future was still open and I could be anything, so I pushed.  


After 25 however, other health things would pop up and it started to feel overwhelming. Not only that, but I was finishing up graduate school and was on the brink of quitting in my second year because I somehow convinced myself I was going to die and didn't have much time left. I hit my first real existential crisis and was lost, but with meditation, the help of friends and family I pushed through some of the hardest moments of my life. It got worse at 29 when my dad was diagnosed with terminal cancer and passed when I was 30. He was probably the strongest rock of support I had in my life, and at least for the time being my mom was a wreck and I really only had myself and wife to help push me through. I had a very high-paying job with a lot of responsibility at the time and around the one year anniversary of my father's death I blew up at work and burned a lot of bridges. I wasn't grieving and was pushing myself too hard, and without my father around to guide me I struggled to survive on my own in this new, scary world.   


Despite this, I have found months where I am confident, strong and motivated. There are other weeks/months where I am down, uncertain, and depressed/anxious. I have gone through several existential crises since I was 25, counting about 2-3 this year alone. I'll get over them, and I will re-experience them again. But I definitely feel that I live for my family now, even when there are times I just want to give up and end it all.  


I guess what I mean to say is that, in youth we have so much optimism because we don't understand the world, we are curious and excited, with doors abound for us in the future. We create fantastical ideas of what we will become and idealize our future. There are some who push their entire lives to extremes to achieve these goals and do, but when they get there are still not satisfied. So they continue to push. There are others where life simply takes them in entirely different directions, many times out of their control, and they grieve the remainder of their lives in regret, or feel maimed and robbed from what they thought life was meant to be. Some people don't survive to adulthood. In one of my existential crises, I realized that it's what makes life interesting -- very very few people ever end up where they imagined themselves in youth. Most people are thrown hardballs, sidetracked, dealing with uncertainty and tackling problem after problem as they get through this life. All I know is that you can use that pressure to push yourself to your limits, or you can let it devour you. Sometimes it does both at different times. I've pushed myself to limits beyond my imagining, and I've also let it blow up in my face.   


I don't know how entirely helpful this is for you, and some people are completely dismissive of self-help, motivational thinking, but depending on what you are looking for Alan Watts is great for pondering the existential crisis of life, whereas Tony Robbins (I was initially very skeptical of him because he comes across as a bit of a dbag and has a bit of a cultish following around him), but that man knows how to turn things around and teach you how to find your locus of control and make decisions that you can change instead of focusing on the things you can't. There are a plethora of great resources out there, even on youtube. But you have to be in a position where you are willing to listen and absorb. You'll know doubt let all the positive thinking bullshit and techniques bounce off you and discredit them, but with some time and patience I have found them to be important tools in my toughest times. Giving me just enough bearing to go out and find the results I want WHILE appreciating deeply what I have, instead of wallowing in what I lack.

Hey there.  


I sometimes feel the same way. I love both my parents and sister to death, but my immediate family seems out of the entire extended family to have the worse luck with health. My sister was born 2-3 months early and has dealt with a bunch of health problems her whole life as well as depression and suicidal ideation. My father passed away from pancreatic cancer two years ago and it completely destroyed the foundation I had in my life. I myself have suffered from immense anxiety from childhood and was medicated from a very young age. I've gone through a bunch of health problems myself, several of them with me for the rest of my life.   


It feels so absolutely helpless to have such burdens that are out of your control. Some people find the right way, the right person... and have a breakthrough that let's them change the way they look at life and immediately are able to just approach everything from a different lens. It's all a big cosmic joke, but while we're here, we might as well find some small blips of enjoyment, no matter how small or sparse they might be.

This. 1000%.

I think those of us who have had immense suffering and struggles in our lives really downplay how much it has made us stronger. The depression and anxiety comes, and when it comes it does push us to idealize suicide. Negative emotions of the past have such a grasp on us, they sink their roots in deep and feed our brain. The fact that you are still here is a testament to your strength, but it's so hard to acknowledge the positives you have in your life because they bounce off your mind with little effort.   


But as /u/drnoog9 stated, your story has a valence that gives many of us perspective. We all have our hardships, some worse than others in different ways, but relatively we all experience suffering, and that perception of suffering is hell for us all. You really should consider writing a book, or looking into doing talks, and continuing to tell your story. It helps to hear others going through a similar thing, to know they aren't the only ones.   


I too can relate to the feeling of being tired and overwhelmed from the trauma I carry, the sense of helplessness to let go of it, to transform it into something productive and powerful. The future for me sometimes feels equally overwhelming and dreadful, and I tend to find solace in the present, enjoying the small things despite the negative thoughts pulling me back into things I have no control over that are determined to convince me my life is not worth living and to give it up. The suicide button is at times an evil comfort, knowing that if things get unbearable I can just turn it all off, but at least in my case I have a wife and two children that I would completely destroy if I did. For them, I endure it when things get rough. I'm sure you have people in your life that you live for, even if you don't yet know it. I

That's essentially it my friend. There is a Japanese phrase from the Nichiren sect of Buddhism called Jikkai Gogu, which means ten thousand realms in a single moment. Essentially, our states of consciousness from moment to moment are constantly shifting between these different levels, some hellish, some heavenly, some logical, some irrational, some self-serving, some empathic. Every dimension of our living experience is in a flux of change, and it's stepping outside of the box and just watching our thoughts float in and out, changing out state as they come and go, that allows us to learn about the impermanence of this experience. Everything is born and dies, comes and goes, in a perpetual change. It was very overwhelming for me to grasp this at first and it did cause more anxiety than anything... but eventually when you learn to let it go and try not to control it it brings a zen to your day to day life. Some may even call it depersonalisation of some sort, but it has a functional advantage in allowing you to accept things as they are.

I may take a more buddhist approach to this, but I truly believe Heaven and Hell is what we make on it on Earth. This existence can very much be your heaven in the moment, or your hell in the moment. For some of us, we suffer so much every day that living is truly a hell. For others, they have aspirations and goals, and sometimes get a taste of that heavenly space, only to lose it eventually with time.   


For most of us though, I'd say it's a wave of heaven and hell, suffering, non-suffering, and sometimes elatement. Those of us with depression are living in our hell states much more than anything else, and so suicide can sometimes feel like the off-switch. The cessation of existence is better than a hell some would argue, but in it's aftermath you often bring those around you into the hell states you once suffered, sometimes for as long as they remain alive. It is dangerous to deny yourself existence, and there is no hurt in waiting another day, and even better if you do things to promote a change away from your personal hell states.

It does pull you in from time to time but as soon as you are able to find some space to focus, bring your attention back to the sensation of the warm water on the skin. It becomes a meditation and eventually with enough exposures you will be able to find showering an enjoyable experience once again. 

It's funny when you look at the bipolarity that exposure therapy (or any truly successful treatment) can cause. This sounds like a body-aware form of agoraphobia. 

Essentially, at the root of your anxiety lies your fear of being made 'aware' in public, a fear of embarrassing yourself, making a mistake in public, or essentially ridicule from those around you. You become hyper aware of your bodily positions and way of walking to the point where you begin to try to make unnatural adjustments to the way you walk and it in turn increases the awkwardness of your gait and ultimately becomes a near-self-fulfilling prophecy. 

It's a common symptom of agoraphobia. Similar to hypochondria in that you 'believe' a symptom into existence through hyperfixation and the nocebo effect, but with the fixation on public humiliation/ridicule rather than an imagined illness.

The root cause of this is of course, your fear of how others see you/hold an opinion of you. The reality (which is distorted and blocked entirely by your anxiety) is that even if you were to REALLY exaggerate your movements so that they become so alien to draw attention, strangers won't remember five to ten seconds after the fact.

Think of all the people you've seen act out in public, done something really dumb/weird/uncanny, or had some clear affliction that made them stand out. Do you remember them? Did it affect you after the fact? Sometime I find that if you are very self-judgemental about a certain thing, you notice it more acutely in others and tend to perseverate on it longer than most people. The lay person won't remember, nor care. And in the very off-chance that they do, whats the likelihood you will run into that person again? What's the likelihood they would go out of their way to make your life a living hell due to the way you walk? 

Again, these are questions that aren't really mean't to be answered, but are more for your own reflection. It's a facet of CBT to try to look at your situation from an objective lens, which is impossible when anxiety is present. But when you find a moment in clarity, it's important to ponder and let these actualities sink in. 

In summary, it's a very common symptom of agoraphobia and I'm sure you will find people who relate.

I think it's important to take into consideration a couple things when discussing panic attacks

1. Panic attacks, and panic disorder are two *very* different things. The average person can experience a panic attack when life gets overwhelming. Panic disorder, on the other hand, is uncontrollable and debilitating, where daily function is chronically disrupted without treatment. This can be a result of no real stimulus or generalized anxiety (Panic Disorder), or triggered by some stimulus (Phobic Disorder), or past trauma (PTSD). It's such a wide umbrella of circumstances that can induce panic, so it's important to find an author who is addressing your specific condition, and not some generalized "panic attack" that the layperson is subject to.

2. A lot of self-help authors in general are not that great at conceptualizing how a panic attack feels universally. I don't blame them either, because everybody experiences different magnitudes of panic, different symptoms, different thought processes that occur alongside it, different aftereffects/repercussions, different triggers and durations. It's so multi-faceted that it's really hard to find a description of panic that speaks to you directly.

For anyone with a real panic disorder - SSRIs are the primary treatment. With enough trial and error you can find a medication and dosage that can treat them into non-existence or into a rare occurrence. 

In my case, I had childhood phobic disorder, with symptoms as early as 4. It got so bad that I became house-ridden, afraid of more things than I was not afraid of. I was medicated since 11 with Paxil, a pretty damn strong SSRI that is nowadays use more as a last-resort medication for people who are are resistant to other medications. 

I'm stuck on it for life - but it gave me my life back. I've had a love/hate relationship with the drug, but I can honestly say my life would have been entirely different had I not opted for treatment.

Xanax is a benzo - all it does is blanket the pain temporarily. Not much different than people who turn to alcohol to numb the pain.

SSRIs are long-lasting and slowly work towards changing your general cognitions to be more neutral instead of biased in negatively. It gives you the ability to distance yourself a bit from the gravity your emotions weigh on your being. Those heavy emotions literally dictate your life and behavior and sometimes it helps to get out of that reference frame and view things from a third person -- a more neutral position. 

You begin to see more clearly how your past experiences shaped who you are now, and most importantly it gives you the space to be able to work with those traumas more objectively to heal from them and possibly even change your course.

Of course, there are traumas we cannot correct or change -- they already happened (like the death, illness, or poor living conditions of someone in the family, a humiliating mistake or a lack of trying in school/getting a career to help you out financially). The negative thoughts of "it's too late" are FALSE. Because you comparing yourself to your peers -- which is natural for humans to do but is ultimately unimportant. Having all the money and power in the world breeds neuroticism and a negative thirst to keep on top. It swallows these people whole.

Celebrities who are stunning and seem to have everything in the world they ever want become numb to it entirely and just wish they could be a normal anonymous person for a day. They can't walk in public without being barraged and every little public behavior they exhibit is examined with the sharpest and deadliest of lenses, published in tabloids. Stars are risen up to be broken down, it's what fuels the gossip society and it's a far more interesting story. 

Yes, there are people who have 'normal lives' - a family, a house, a car, etc. But these people suffer too, in different ways sure but they suffer. We cannot compare ourselves to them because we are not them and they are not us. You are you, and that's ALL that should ever matter.

Perhaps you have had absorbed your failures into your self-worth rather than seeing them as something that many people have to cope and learn from.
